Name: -1_plow_farm_manor_horses
Representative_Docs:
["Tiny little birds,  
Let's go blossom, little flowers.  
At the cattle gathering, the hoofs.  
We are justified in blooming.  
At the cattle gathering, there is shouting!  
At the bloom, the beer is red.  
At the cattle gathering, the kvass is sour.  
Where are we going, the six of us,  
Over the field - five of us,  
Over the meadow, four of us.  
In front is a long boundary forest,  
Behind a wide board forest,  
In between, a maple tree forest,  
The sky is wide and open,  
The night is long and dark. –  
Young girls, young men:  
Let's go over the five fields,  
There sits a beautiful chamberlain,  
A white veiled chamber,  
The wind sweeps the chamber doors.  
There are many German houses,  
Many young gentlemen's houses,  
They wanted to make a bed there,  
To put pillows for sleeping.  
From there I secretly came out,  
A little sneaky – a little sneaking,  
I gave the door an elbow,  
Whistled a tune for the kvass.  
So that the doors wouldn't open,  
The birch twigs shouted,  
I ran home myself.  
Who met me on the way?  
Met were the Germans of Valga,  
Met were the old gentlemen of Valga.  
In front of them were burrows, little tunnels,  
Among them old hares –  
Behind them iron carts.  
In the middle, the handsome foxes.  
I asked for a whip to hit the dog,  
To tear the collar away. –  
They did not give a whip to hit the dog,  
Did not allow to tear the collar.  
Then I took a long rowan twig,  
A little bird cherry stick.  
At the front, I struck the burrows, the tunnels,  
Among them the old hares,  
From behind the iron carts.  
I ran home myself,  
I was not allowed to sleep at home,  
While I was at the feast –  
For two nights I slept on the oat straw.", 'The man did not want a wife for me  
The lord did not give a good dowry,  
The brother did not forge a copper ring,  
The sister did not knit a mitten.  
My family wanted me to be a soldier,  
Brothers to become Russian men.  
I do not want to be a soldier,  
Nor do I want to become a Russian man.  
I am a bad drudge,  
Chosen to bark against,  
A black hay mower,  
A hunchbacked ploughman:  
I leave the hills unploughed,  
The flower beds uncultivated.  
It’s harsh to walk the road,  
Misery is the lord’s legacy.  
The road is shown with a stick,  
Given a piece of garden weed.  
In the manor, fields are measured,  
Additional fields are rented,  
Many fields are offered.  
Today I drink in the tavern, tomorrow in the tavern,  
On Sunday I drink without pants.  
Monday is for sleeping,  
Tuesday is to go to the road.  
Wednesday to carry stones,  
Thursday to make wheat,  
Friday to cut sticks,  
Saturday to saw beams.  
Hooray, hurrah! we shout,  
We break men down  
We catch girls!  
In the tavern I drink a little,  
To the small town, to the gray one.  
To the linen town road,  
To the market, red-faced,  
To the fair a little bit,  
Always money for barn planks.  
I have no money at home!  
With me is walking money,  
In my vest pocket is vodka money,  
In my boot shaft is bread money,  
By the wall is standing money,  
In the barn is gray gelding money,  
In the stable the money for a spotted cow.  
In the sack is pocket money,  
From last year the money for a black bull,  
From the year before the money for a polecat.', 'Oh, this poor Tapa parish,  
The hungry Näu village,  
Where I don’t dare to walk in the manor,  
I don’t flash before the lord:  
I don’t even have a barley cake in my pocket,  
Nor any oat porridge in my pan.  
Salt is scarce inside the box,  
And beer is thin in the neck.  
Women walk the manor roads  
Wearing egg mittens.  
Pairs of chickens in the stall,  
Pairs of geese under the hem.  
Thread scarves in their hands,  
The court’s sheep on the hilltop  
Are led out into the manor yard  
To the old lord on the rampart.  
From there the lord comes grunting:  
“Look where the poor sheep stands.  
Take it home to the dogs,  
Give it to the hound!  
Bring me a fatty from the barn,  
A pretty one from the herd  
To carry to the manor’s sheepfold.”  
When the people go to work:  
The coachman goes like a devil,  
The young lord like Judas behind;  
The parish like a prisoner in the middle.  
Then you hear the coachman’s voice,  
The old lord’s cursing.  
There the rowan struggles,  
And then the fir tree moves  
And there the bird cherry staggers  
Over the shoulder of the apple tree.  
But it strikes past the fine coat,  
Past the thin shoulders,  
Past the long sleeves.  
The tenant sighs in slave bondage,  
A tear in his eye.  
The coachman is called hell,  
The young lord is sent after,  
The old lord to watch.  
Tables are set in place,  
Chairs are brought to the table,  
Fire and tar also brought:  
Eat, coachman, drink, steward,  
This poor parish’s toil,  
Its tiny pain-blood.  
If you tormented the parish,  
If you tormented the little ones.  
Oh, this golden Kuruda,  
Silver Roosnaida,  
When the people went to work:  
The coachman like the moon,  
The young lord like God behind,  
The parish like copper in the middle.  
No fir moves there,  
Nor does the rowan struggle.  
No bird cherry staggers there,  
Over the shoulder of the apple tree.  
No sound of the coachman’s voice,  
Nor the steward’s whining,  
Nor the old lord’s cursing.']

Name: 0_hay_granny_little grandmother_pasture
Representative_Docs:
["Our two poor peasants  
Let's go to Midsummer at the church  
Let's go to the grandmother's grave  
Let's go to the grandfather's grave  
Put the sorrow handkerchiefs on  
Put the sorrow apples in the handkerchief  
Rise up, little grandmother  
Rise up, little grandfather  
Rise up to braid my hair  
To prepare the grain container  
To fasten the coffin lid.  
But the woman answered, the man replied  
You cannot rise, young daughter  
You cannot rise, do not wake up  
Grass had grown over the soil  
Branch hay over the grave  
Coltsfoot on the eyebrows  
Bluebells on the eyes  
Marigolds at the feet.  
Still rise, little grandmother  
Still rise, little grandfather  
Rise up to braid my hair.  
I feed grass to the calves  
Hay to the oxen  
Coltsfoot to the roosters  
Bluebells to the pigs  
Marigolds to the calves.", 'Our two mourners  
Let's go to the midsummer church  
Handkerchiefs in hand  
Mourning cloths on the head  
One cries, the other cries  
One wipes the other's eyes  
One strokes the other's head  
Let's go to grandmother's grave  
Let's go to grandfather's grave  
"Rise up, little grandmother,  
Rise to comb my head,  
To prepare the gift basket,  
To fasten the kerchief."  
"You must not rise, young daughter,  
You must not rise, do not awaken:  
Grass has grown over the soil,  
Hay grown over the grave;  
Apple trees over the straw,  
Bluebells over the eyes,  
Coltsfoot over the eyebrows,  
Linden trees over the hair.  
Feed the grass to the young bullocks,  
The hay to the oxen,  
The bluebells to the cows."  
"Still rise, little grandmother;  
I will bring a sand sieve from the town,  
From the market, a fine sieve,  
From the borough, a coarse sieve,  
I would sift the sieve with fine grains,  
Roll it with fine sand."  
The grandmother hears, replies:  
"You must not rise, do not awaken,  
May God comb your head,  
May the Creator fasten your kerchief,  
Prepare the gift basket."  
"Then I go home crying:  
A speckled bird was on the kerchief,  
A white bird was on the basket.  
I would like to thank:  
To God for grandmother's soul,  
To God for grandfather's soul,  
Hands into Mary's hands,  
Heart into Jesus' lap,  
Knees into the Creator's earth."', "Our Two Poor Children  
Let's go to the Midsummer Day church  
Let's go to grandmother's grave;  
Let's go to grandfather's grave.  
Rise up, dear grandmother,  
Rise up, dear grandfather,  
Rise to comb my hair,  
To prepare Annivakka,  
To fasten the coffin lid.  

You must not rise, young daughter,  
You must not rise, do not awaken.  
Grass has grown over the soil,  
Field herbs upon the grave,  
Bluebells on the eyes,  
Coltsfoot on the eyebrows,  
Marsh marigold at the feet,  
Wild berries on the toes.  

You must not rise, young daughter,  
You must not rise, do not awaken.  
May God comb your hair,  
May He prepare Annivakka.  
Still rise, dear grandmother,  
I will feed the grass to the calves,  
Field herbs to the oxen,  
Bluebells to the cows.  

Oh, our two poor children,  
Let's go to the Midsummer Day church.  
I am going to grandmother's grave,  
You are going to grandfather's grave.  

Rise up, dear grandfather,  
Rise up, dear grandmother,  
Rise to comb my hair,  
To prepare Annivakka,  
To fasten the coffin lid.  

But grandmother understood and grandfather answered:  
Grass has grown over the soil,  
Field herbs upon the grave,  
Coltsfoot on the eyebrows,  
Bluebells on the eyes,  
Marsh marigolds at the feet.  

Still rise, dear grandfather,  
Still rise, dear grandmother.  
I will feed the grass to the calves,  
Field herbs to the oxen,  
Coltsfoot to the roosters,  
Bluebells to the pigs,  
Marsh marigold to the calves."]

Name: 1_hops_hop_beer_drinks
Representative_Docs:
["Hops called me into the ditch,  
Cone creaked into the corner stove  
Come here, young men,  
Take me to the hut of the bear,  
Make me a steed for the stag,  
Put me to dry on the railing.  
From there I go to the barn,  
Slip into the half-pint of beer,  
Roll between the twigs;  
Then I take the senses from men's heads,  
Half the senses from boys' heads,  
Thanks from wise women's heads;  
Men roar without hats,  
Women dance without the ground,  
Boys half without boots,  
Girls without belts.", "In the hollow, a pine cone calls into the stream  
A cone crackles into the bush  
In the grassy rye field  
Come here, young men  
Take me to the sack at home  
Set me on the bench by the stove  
Put me on the board to dry  
From there I roll into the cellar  
But I slip into the half-beer glass  
Drift into the beer mug  
Sink into the beer anchor  
Make me a good beer  
That takes away men's senses  
Half of the senses from the boys' heads  
Thanks to wise women's heads  
Men grumble without hats  
Women dance without cloth  
Girls without belts  
Boys with crooked backs  
One drinks from one hand to the other  
Mothers-in-law, mothers with buckets  
Look, I drink from the pail  
I feed my head through the pipe  
Do I drink from the cupboard, or from the jug  
Or do I drink from the colorful cup  
The cone makes the eyes colorful  
The jug makes the neck stiff.", "A little beer, a little beauty,  
A little ale, a little darling,  
From your face, you are the handsome one,  
From your stomach, you are the sweet one.  
You walk along my stomach,  
March along my belly,  
Stretch along the spine.  
Be healthy, brewers!  
Who made good beer,  
Often went to the tavern,  
Sometimes went to the well.  
But I sip along with my mind,  
I try along the edge of the pitcher.  
The hop calls in the stream,  
The cone crackles in the bush:  
Come, come young men,  
Pick me into your sack,  
Take me out for the work in the field,  
Put me on the bench edge,  
Carry me to the kitchen stove!  
Then I rise onto the loft,  
I swell along the long gutter.  
Then I take the minds of men,  
Half the minds of the boys' heads,  
The temples from the women's foreheads.  
Men make noise without hats,  
Women dance without shoes,  
Boys half kneeling.  
The beer was wild and the bottle was smart,  
Ale was very sly.  
Oh, you proud barley water,  
Oh, you wrathful grain water,  
Though you surely bring me down,  
Still, I take you inside me."]

Name: 2_ends_harvest_end_grain
Representative_Docs:
['End, end, little field  
Come to an end, little island  
You have long been started.  
And long ago they began cutting you  
Every day they came to you.  
Every hour they came to your roots  
Rise up, sisters, truly  
Hold up the anger because  
We swim to the ends  
We reach the island’s edge  
The red beer is finished  
There are milk cakes in the barn.  
There are slender breads on the island  
So let me say it again  
Let me sing the words back.  
Maybe the slave whip is at an end  
There is a slave whip in the barn  
There are slave pains on the island.', 'Surely I will reap, but I am exhausted  
I do not understand what is with me  
Has my strength been taken  
Or are my hands tied  
Fingers tied in knots,  
Is my head braided?  
Or is there rust on this sickle?  
The sickle was made by an evil smith  
The sickle is wicked, not his whole  
The iron is rusty, not his cutting,  
The sickle was made by an evil smith,  
The iron has become rusted,  
A crooked paw has broken.  
Oh, you barley squirrel,  
And you, cunning oats.  
And you, rye rummager,  
And you, leats, pig herders:  
Why did you grow wicked,  
Why did you rise from low ground  
To bow to my gold,  
To bend your gentle back?  
May your back break,  
May your neck crack.  
On your large fields,  
On the bottomless fields.  
Here the hunchbacked have plowed,  
The edge has nibbled the root,  
Sown the piglets,  
And driven the rowdies wild.  
If only they had plowed a gentle brother,  
And tilled a humble sister.  
Then willows would grow thicker  
And reeds lie down.  
Now I reap the pig’s mess,  
The goose’s bad trampling,  
The crane’s evil turning,  
For you have only the crane’s quilt left,  
The crane’s quilt, the grouse’s cover,  
The gray goose’s mantle.  
Here pigs have slept,  
Geese have swum for a year,  
A flock of ducks have paddled.', 'End, end, little field  
Come to an end, little island  
Diminish, diminish, go away  
For you have long been cut down  
Long ago cut down, dried out  
Every day they walked on you  
Every hour they came to you  
Come, come, little wind  
Blessing, dear Creator’s wind  
Take the water from the grain  
The dew from the oat stalk  
Rust from the top of the grass  
So that I may reap a sheaf of grain  
Two sheaves with dew  
Three sheaves with the dawn.']

Name: 3_young maiden_maiden young_maiden_maidens
Representative_Docs:
['Virgin girl, young maiden,  
Do not go to a young man as a husband,  
To an ungrown mate.  
You think he will help you grow,  
You think he will help you grow,  
But he gives only a man’s mind?  
A mate does not help growth,  
But a man takes away your mind;  
A mate asks for cloth from a weaver,  
But a man asks for clothes from a tailor:  
Every month he wants a new hat,  
Every week he wants four shirts,  
Every day he wants something fine,  
Every noon he wants linen.  
If you do not give it to him,  
Then you shall feel the whip,  
And you shall taste the rod:  
The man warns with his arm –  
You respond with your leg,  
Your mouth to your big toe:  
"Oh, legs, keep moving, legs,  
Keep me from beating,  
Keep me from the lash of the whip!"', 'I saw the maiden growing;
By the blue fence
Swelling with a red wreath;
Rising in a tin crown.
I, from the stables;
From the coal-black haven,
From the window I gave barley,
In the shadows I carried water;
Without the old woman's knowledge,
Without the old man's knowledge,
That I gained the horse's strength.
In front I put sturdy irons;
Behind irons from the threshing floor.
Then I harnessed the horse.
After that I put on the bridle,
On top I put a playful bow,
Eyes into silk reins,
Eyebrows into golden rings,
Tail into a braid,
Brushed the mane to one side.
I rode to the father-in-law's door,
I rode to the mother-in-law's door:
"Hello, father-in-law! Boot-tops,
Hello, mother-in-law! Neck of the kettle,
Are your maidens at home?"
The mother-in-law understood, answered:
"Our daughters are at the well,
Drawing water at the well."
I ride to the well road:
"Hello, dear maiden!
Drawing water with the bucket,
To water all the village's herd;
To water my horse at the well.
Let my black one paw,
Let my gray one sway,
Let my dappled one tug,
Move on the linen cloth.
I, a poor wayfarer,
Wayfarer, knower of lands;
Lord of matters,
Messenger of kings,
Keeper of the town council's book,
A postman from St. Petersburg."
The maiden hears, answers again:
"You are not a poor wayfarer,
Wayfarer, knower of lands,
Lord of matters,
Messenger of kings,
Keeper of the town council's book,
Postman from St. Petersburg.
You are an evil suitor,
And a deceitful groom:
Why is your horse harnessed?
Brushed mane and swayed tail?
Why do you have locks on the bridle?
Why do you have an eagle's skull?
A headgear in the harness?
A sparrow in the reins?"
I heard, answered again,
"I have at home an old father
Who makes the locks on the bridle.
I have at home a little brother
Who is my horse's groom,
Brushed mane and swayed tail.
He puts the tail in a braid,
Eyes in silk reins,
Ears in golden rings.
I have at home a little sister
Who makes the letters on gloves
Who makes lace on the whip..."', "Virgin girl, young maiden,  
Let us go to the young man,  
Unmatured companion.  
You think of nurturing,  
Giving manly mind.  
A companion does not make one mature,  
A man does not take the mind.  
But the companion asks for cloth,  
The man asks for fine clothes.  
Every month wants a new coat,  
Every week wants four shirts,  
Every day wants something delicate,  
Every noon wants linen.  
If you do not give this to her,  
Then you will feel torment,  
And you will taste bitterness.  
The man informs the flame.  
I inform the foot,  
The mouth to the big toe.  
But hold me back from it,  
From the whip's straps on my head."]

Name: 4_little bird_rooster_hen went_chickens
Representative_Docs:
['Raven, gentle little bird,  
Laid eggs under our hill.  
In the nest came out five chicks.  
One became a handsome father,  
Another became a calm mother,  
The third became a puppy boy,  
The fourth became a wheat guard,  
The fifth a playful fellow.  
The playful fellow was the cleverest.  
He went to town to bring a wife:  
In the small town, he played a pipe,  
In the market square, he beat a drum,  
So that the walls shook,  
The floor beams rattled,  
Pots broke on the fire,  
Pots broke in the shop.  
Then the poor man began to stumble,  
The man with tight pants began to weave.  
The captors came,  
The reins in the seeker’s hand,  
The rope with the captor.  
I would tear apart the rope’s threads,  
Tear the reins to the end.  
Then the man with tight pants began to weave,  
Across the field, across the field,  
Sometimes along the fence in the yard.  
What will come against me?  
Then came to the golden spruce forest,  
Then to the low pine forest,  
Then to the rare open forest,  
Then I went through the alder forest.  
Then I gave power to my hands,  
Then I gave power to my feet,  
Power, power to my toes:  
Row your legs, reach your hands.', "Little rooster, little hen!
You went off running in a race.
The rooster went under the rich man's thigh,
The hen to the poor man's barn.
The rooster got one barley ear.
The hen got two oat grains.
They put a plank on top,
Rolled it to the mill.
They paid Matt the miller,
And the other to the trash heap owner.
They started making beer.
Got a pig's horn full,
A mother's goat's ear full.", "The rooster and the hen together  
went to the barn to peck,  
to peck at the neck of the barn.  
The rooster found three barley grains,  
the hen two oats grains.  
- Let's roll to the mill,  
let's make oilless soot;  
we call together the sad birds,  
we gather the bad birds.  
We do not call the little hawk,  
nor the hawk's wife,  
The hawk was angry at the rooster,  
the hawk's wife at the hen;  
they tore the crane's new nest,  
the swallow's headgear,  
the woodpecker's jaws apart."]

Name: 5_mistress little_servant_little mistress_servants
Representative_Docs:
["Master, little master,  
Mistress, little mistress:  
Pay the servant well,  
Reward the poor child's toil.  
If you do not pay in this world,  
Surely you will pay in heaven,  
You will pay before Mary.  
Surely you will walk to the stocks,  
March to the whipping post,  
The fabric to the broad loom.  
Come, then, pay the servant wages,  
The servant’s summer wages,  
A day’s full day’s wages.  
Then I understand, I reply:  
I do not want to go to heaven  
If I was not paid in that world,  
Where the breastbone was broken,  
The neckbone snapped,  
And many other bones broken.", 'Master, little master,  
Mistress, little lady,  
Pay well the servant’s wage,  
Compensate the poor child’s toil.  
If you do not pay in this world,  
Then you will pay in heaven,  
(You pay before Mary)  
You will be at the mercy of the elbow tree,  
You will march to the shoulder of the whip tree,  
The cloth to wide tension.  

"Come now, servant, take your pay,  
Servant—winter pay,  
Day laborer—daily wage."  

Then I understand, I answer:  
"I do not want to go to heaven,  
If I was not paid in that world,  
Where the ribs were broken,  
Where the neck bones were fractured,  
And many other bones were broken too."', "I was a slave, I tended the herd  
I was a Dutch servant,  
A shepherd boy from the land of souls,  
What was my wage for the dyke path?  
An old coat, an old fur coat,  
Are you satisfied with that?  
And are you satisfied with us?  
I do not agree to that  
Nor am I satisfied with you.  
If I serve, I will serve still  
A rich man and the well-mannered.  

I was a slave, I tended the herd  
I was a Dutch servant,  
A shepherd boy from the land of souls,  
What was my wage for the dyke path?  
An old rag on a shriveled branch,  
An old bundle at the edge of the forest,  
Do you agree to that?  
And are you satisfied with us?  
I do not agree to that  
Nor am I satisfied with you.  
If I serve, I will serve still  
A rich man and the well-mannered.  

I was a slave, I tended the herd  
I was a Dutch servant,  
A shepherd boy from the land of souls,  
What was my wage for the dyke path?  
A sheep with a lamb,  
A pig with a hundred piglets,  
Do you agree to that?  
And are you satisfied with us?  
I am not satisfied with that  
Nor do I agree with you.  
If I serve, I will serve still  
A rich man and the well-mannered.  

I was a slave, I tended the herd  
I was a Dutch servant,  
A shepherd boy from the land of souls,  
What was my wage for the dyke path?  
A horse with the largest bridle,  
A barn with a hundred horned heads,  
Do you agree, do you agree with that?  
And are you satisfied with us?  
I do not agree to that  
Nor am I satisfied with you.  
If I serve, I will serve still  
A rich man and the well-mannered.  

I was a slave, I tended the herd  
I was a Dutch servant,  
A shepherd boy from the land of souls,  
What was my wage for the dyke path?  
From Tallinn to the roads of Tartu,  
The big cities of the land of Finland,  
Do you agree to that?  
And are you satisfied with us?  
I do not agree to that  
Nor am I satisfied with you.  
If I serve, I will serve still  
A rich man and the well-mannered.  

I was a slave, I tended the herd  
I was a Dutch servant,  
A shepherd boy from the land of souls,  
What was my wage for the dyke path?  
A virgin's bed of gold,  
Supply all the house tools,  
Do you agree to that?  
And are you satisfied with us?  
Yes, I agree to that

Name: 6_dung_wet pine_little bird_reeds
Representative_Docs:
['The lark sings on the tile  
The swallow at the edge of the border  
Where is your darling’s nest?  
In the forest on top of a dry spruce.  
Which spruce?  
An old man cut the spruce.  
Which old man?  
The old man died.  
When was he buried?  
In the long field’s garden bed.  
Which garden bed?  
A hen scratched the garden bed.  
Which hen?  
The hen flew into the grass.  
What grass?  
A sickle mowed the grass.  
Which sickle?  
The sickle’s edge is worn.  
Which edge?  
A bear gnawed the edge.  
Which bear?  
The bear swam across the sea.  
Which sea?  
A black bull drank from the sea.  
Wh-  
The black bull went to the barn.  
Which barn?  
The fire burned in the barn.  
Which fire?  
The fire went to the sky,  
With pots, pans,  
Spatulas, spoons.', 'Liiri-lõõri little flute  
Piiri-pääri little swallow  
Where is your golden nest?  
In the forest on a dry fir tree  
Where did that dry fir come from?  
An old man cut the fir down  
Where did that old man come from?  
The old man died  
Where was he buried?  
In the long bed of the field  
Where did that field bed come from?  
Oxen plowed it up  
Where did those oxen come from?  
A bear broke them down  
Where did that bear come from?  
The bear went to the long reeds  
Where did those reeds come from?  
A sickle mowed them down  
Where did that sickle come from?

Name: 9_horse_horses_stallions_stallion
Representative_Docs:
['I fell asleep on the hill of dreams  
I ended up below a steep shore  
Here is a room made of tulips  
Eaves made of curls.  
Here is a ceiling of glass  
Walls of silk ribbons  
Repairs here are made of paper.  
Here I lie down to rest  
To rest for a moment  
To doze for an hour or two  
To strengthen myself with a scrap,  
Now is the time for warmth  
I will rise with the morning  
Then will come winter snow and cold  
My horse is still unfound  
German sleigh not prepared.  
White reins disregarded.  
Then I went to find the stable  
I found the horse in the field  
The German sleigh on the manure  
White reins at the end of the pole.  
Then I put on the mouse-gray ones  
Pulled the crane-neck over the ear  
Then I went to drive on the bog  
And to make a path to the field  
Whether bridges were made over the bog  
Paths made to the field  
Bridges made from onions  
Half the bridges from carrots  
No one gets their foot wet there  
No one gets their foot wet, no ox gets dirty  
The rooster does not wear golden spurs  
The hen does not have copper combs  
Then I rode along the Finnish bridge  
My horse underneath like a furnace  
On the groom like this day  
Bridge beams for the breakers  
Under beams for the cracklers  
Groom’s hat for the drummers  
Wide ribbons waving.', 'I fed the stallion, I gave the stallion to drink...  
I went to the German's matchmaker,  
I sent the Germans to Saaremaa,  
The lords to Hiiumaa,  
Half the gentlemen to Poland.  
I started coming home,  
I found a tavern down a lane.  
I went to take a drink,  
I took one drink, I took two,  
I went to take a third drink,  
A thief came from the grove,  
Another from outside the yard,  
They took my good horses,  
A ten-ruble hat,  
A hundred-ruble saddle.  
I came home crying,  
Weeping outside in the yard;  
The woman was there, the man was there,  
Both the old ones answered.  
"Why do you cry, young son?  
We have three stallions at home,  
One is a gold-maned stallion,  
The second is silver-maned,  
The third bronze maned."  
"Well, we will give them for you,  
Redeem you from this trouble."  
...  
I fed the stallion, I gave the stallion to drink,  
The stallion gained strength indeed.  
I went to Koigi to court,  
To the smith Koigi’s daughters  
Were quite famous maidens.  
One was Anne, another Kaie,  
The third a sweet Maiekene.  
Anne was given to me,  
Kaie was bargained for me.  
Ann was naked by the stove,  
Kai was bare bottomed by the rack,  
Mai was on the threshing floor,  
A sack underneath her, and a sack on top,  
A piece of sack by her side,  
No way to bring her home.  
I came home crying,  
The woman was there, the man was there,  
Both the old ones answered.  
"Why do you cry, young son?  
- Why not cry, old woman!  
Why not cry, old man!  
I fed the stallion, I gave it to drink,  
The stallion gained strength and stamina.  
I went to Koigi to court,  
To the smith Koigi’s daughters  
Cannot bring them home,  
I left them out as wild ones,  
The garden barn as helpers!"  
...  
The woman was there, the man was there,  
Both the old ones answered.  
"Why do you cry, young son?  
Bring home the announced wife!  
Set her on the table!  
If not, she will take the lower place,  
She will manage the household affairs,  
She will rinse the spoon handle."', 'I was a slave, I tended the herd  
I was in the Dutch service  
In the fields of Lehila's sheep  
Holland made a new dome  
Lehila land a wide coat.  
Oh, poor me, a prisoner of children  
Complained from the hiding place!  
Nights I am imprisoned, nights I am saved.  
Nights I keep watch over my father’s herd  
I protect the herd of my brother  
At the river mouth, at the lake mouth  
In the middle of the river’s whirlpool  
Between the river’s currents.  
Two merchants came  
Two merchant servants  
Both had swords at their belts  
Both had spurs on their feet.  
"Maiden, young girl  
In embroidered clothing, slender,  
Sell me father’s horse  
Trade for brother’s saddle."  
"I will not sell father’s herd  
I will not trade brother’s saddle  
Father has a good horse,  
Brother has a dear saddle."  
"Sell me the sword at your belt  
Trade for the spurs on your feet."  
"I will not sell the sword at my belt  
I will not trade the spurs on my feet  
Maiden, young girl  
Allow me to come to you,  
To come to you until death  
To be with you until the end of life.  
I will put you to easy work:  
Beating rye stalks  
Treading on oat husks.  
In summer I keep smoke away  
In winter I lift dust away.  
In summer I feed you sugar rushes  
In winter buckwheat tangles,  
A year's goose meat.

"I hear, I answer:

Pumpkins for goose meat."  
"Allow me to come  
To come to you, to stay with you."  
"Maybe you would bake me in gold  
Spin silk threads  
Sew with silver thread.  
Maybe there would be a silver yard  
An iron-forged gate  
Stone in the corral,  
Still I will not come to you.  
For you a pigsty  
A horse’s nightmare,  
A dog’s snout with a stick in it  
A mouth like a poor man’s hole  
Face like a paper sack  
Teeth like cattle gates  
Jaws like that of a tongs.  
I will go where it is created  
Where the Creator has made a place  
Mary has given a home.  
Where my blood has carried  
Where my color has taken me  
Where my little luck shares in.  
Maybe there would be an oily yard  
Maybe a fenced garden  
Gates forged from twigs,  
Maybe there would be a pillar in the yard  
In the corral stone stakes  
Still I go where it is created,  
Where the Creator has made a place,  
Mary has given a home.  
Where my blood has carried  
Where my color has taken me  
Where my little luck shares in."']

Name: 29_sorrow_sorrowful_wretched_torment
Representative_Docs:
["I am bored

To the stone on the church road

I live for the meadowsweet  
I lament to the bluebells  
The coltsfoots turn yellow  
The meadowsweets droop  
The bluebells wilt;  
At my sorrow to my dear  
And my restlessness to my friend  
Wiping my delicate eyes  
Because I am bored  
Always restless  
Many times my spirits are sad  
I had a father when I was young  
A mother when I was born  
I am the son of a horse  
The little child of a wild stallion.  
The horse nursed me  
As I licked the wild stallion.", 'When I begin to go  
Then sorrow begins to come  
Water rolling from the eyes  
I do not forget beauty  
I do not fear dear joy  
I take beauty with me  
Joy between the clothes  
Fun in six folds  
Jokes in the scarlet flax  
Then the corners remained wet from crying  
Father’s horses neighing  
Cattle bellowing  
Grandmother’s punished cows crying  
Good feeders crying  
Feeders, waterers  
Those who give hay before  
Those who bring oats by hand  
Those who raise rye flowers  
I serve bitter work  
I till the evil fields  
Frugal, neat chamber  
Work had to be done, toil endured  
Water twisted from the sleeve  
Turned from six courses  
I do not understand bitter thanks  
The wicked did not give warning  
All my fingers were scolded  
Forearms bruised  
I understand, I answer back  
If only my yards were rowans  
Shoulders like orchards  
Forearms like maples  
Fingers in currant leaves  
Then I should accept punishment  
Would take the beating sticks  
Would endure the strike blows  
Before the harsh scoldings  
The most stern nods  
Pass through my heart  
Through my beautiful body  
Through my red face  
Through my tangled hair  
Whom I show dullness  
Or to whom I complain of sad mind  
To the stone on the church path  
To the lime on the lime wall outside  
The stone was stubborn, would not speak  
The lime was thick, would not chat  
The stone did not understand the girl’s refusal  
The lime did not grant the girl’s request  
Little stone, little rock  
Little lime, plump one  
You could have lived in the sea  
Vanished on the seashore  
Before you came to our land  
To torment me  
To trouble my hands', "Always I am sorrowful

To whom do I set sorrow
